summary: Describes RSA and DSA key and signature encoding, and binary key encoding, for version 2 of the KeyNote trust-management system. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo says exactly how a public key or a signature is written down in the KeyNote trust management system, and what a program should compare when it decides whether two keys are the same. It also reserves a set of short names, such as rsa-base64 and sig-dsa-sha1-hex, so that two programs reading the same credential will understand it in the same way.

subtitle: How KeyNote writes down RSA and DSA keys and signatures, so that every implementation reads them the same way.

tldr.problem: KeyNote identifies people and programs by their public keys, but the same key can be written in more than one way. A key in base64 in one credential and the same key in hexadecimal in another must still be recognised as one key.
tldr.mechanism: Every key type has a normalized form that defines what the key really is, and an encoding that puts it on the wire. An RSA key is an ASN.1 SEQUENCE of two INTEGERs, a DSA key a SEQUENCE of four, and a binary identifier has no internal structure. Each is then written as hex or base64 text behind a name that says which.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and defines no standard. It reserves twelve algorithm identifiers for IANA, and leaves the security of KeyNote itself to RFC 2704.

today: RFC 2792 is an Informational memo from March 2000 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the key and signature encodings for the KeyNote system defined in RFC 2704, and reserves the algorithm identifiers those encodings use.

sections.title: Why Keys Need an Encoding
sections.content:
KeyNote is a simple and flexible trust-management system designed to work well for a variety of large- and small-scale Internet-based applications. It provides a single, unified language for both local policies and credentials. KeyNote policies and credentials, called assertions, contain predicates that describe the trusted actions permitted by the holders of specific public keys. A signed assertion, which can be sent over an untrusted network, is also called a credential assertion. Credential assertions, which also serve the role of certificates, have the same syntax as policy assertions but are also signed by the principal delegating the trust. The KeyNote system itself is defined in RFC 2704, and this memo assumes reader familiarity with it.

Cryptographic keys may be used in KeyNote to identify principals. To facilitate interoperation between different implementations and to allow for maximal flexibility, keys must be converted to a normalized canonical form, which depends on the public key algorithm used, for the purposes of any internal comparisons between keys. An RSA key may be encoded in base64 ASCII in one credential and in hexadecimal ASCII in another, and an implementation must internally convert the two encodings to a normalized form that allows comparison between them. Furthermore, the internal structure of an encoded key must be known for an implementation to correctly decode it.

In some applications, other types of values, such as a passphrase or a random nonce, may be used as principal identifiers. When these identifiers contain characters that may not appear in a string, a simple ASCII encoding is necessary to allow their use inside KeyNote assertions. If the identifier only contains characters that can appear in a string, it may be used as it is. Such identifiers may not be used to sign an assertion, and so no related signature encoding is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: A public key is a long number, and there are several ways to write a long number down as text. This memo picks one structure for each kind of key and one way of writing it, so that a program can take apart what it reads and compare it with another key.

sections.title: Normalized Forms
sections.content:
Comparisons always happen between normalized forms, and the memo defines three of them.

  • A DSA key is identified by four values: the public value y, and the p, q and g parameters. These four values together make up the DSA key normalized form used in KeyNote, and all DSA key comparisons occur between normalized forms.
  • An RSA key is identified by two values: the public exponent and the modulus. These two values together make up the RSA key normalized form, and all RSA key comparisons occur between normalized forms.
  • A binary identifier has as its normalized form the identifier's data itself, so binary identifier comparisons are essentially binary-string comparisons of the identifier values.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of key has a short list of numbers that really defines it. Two keys are the same when those numbers match, however they were written down. For a passphrase, the data itself is the definition, so two binary identifiers are compared as plain strings.

sections.title: Key Encoding
sections.content:
A DSA key is encoded as an ASN1 SEQUENCE of four ASN1 INTEGER objects: the public value, then the p, q and g parameters of the DSA key, in that order. For use in KeyNote credentials, the ASN1 SEQUENCE is then ASCII-encoded, for example as a string of hex digits or base64 characters. DSA keys encoded this way in KeyNote must be identified by the dsa-XXX: algorithm name, where XXX is the ASCII encoding, either hex or base64. Other ASCII encoding schemes may be defined in the future.

An RSA key is encoded as an ASN1 SEQUENCE of two ASN1 INTEGER objects: the public exponent and the modulus, in that order. The memo's text here calls the modulus part of the DSA key, which appears to be a slip. The ASN1 SEQUENCE is then ASCII-encoded in the same way, and such keys must be identified by the rsa-XXX: algorithm name, where XXX is hex or base64.

Binary identifiers are assumed to have no internal encoding and are treated as a sequence of binary digits. They are ASCII-encoded similarly to RSA and DSA keys, and must be identified by the binary-XXX: algorithm name, where XXX is hex or base64.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key becomes a short list of big numbers, written in a standard structured form and then turned into letters and digits. A label at the front says what kind of key it is and which alphabet was used, so a reader knows how to undo the transformation.

sections.title: Signatures
sections.content:
Both DSA and RSA signatures are computed over the assertion body, which starts at the beginning of the first keyword and runs up to and including the newline character immediately before the Signature: keyword, and over the signature algorithm name, including its trailing colon character, for example sig-dsa-sha1-base64:. Including the algorithm name in what is signed means a signature cannot be moved from one algorithm to another.

A DSA signature is encoded as an ASN1 SEQUENCE of two ASN1 INTEGER objects, the r and s values of a DSA signature, in that order. The ASN1 SEQUENCE is then ASCII-encoded as a string of hex digits or base64 characters, and must be identified by the sig-dsa-XXX-YYY: algorithm name, where XXX is a hash function name and YYY is the ASCII encoding. SHA1 is currently the only hash function that may be used with DSA.

An RSA signature is encoded as an ASN1 OCTET STRING object containing the signature value. The OCTET STRING is then ASCII-encoded in the same way, and must be identified by the sig-rsa-XXX-YYY: algorithm name, where XXX is a hash function name and YYY is the ASCII encoding. Either MD5 or SHA1 may be used with RSA.

Binary identifiers are unstructured sequences of binary digits and are not associated with any cryptographic algorithm, so they may not be used to validate an assertion. That is why the memo defines no signature encoding for them.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature covers the text of the credential and the name of the algorithm that produced it. It is then written down in the same structured form as a key, and its name says which hash function was used and which alphabet the result is in. Because a passphrase has no algorithm behind it, it cannot sign anything.

sections.title: Reserved Identifiers and Security
sections.content:
Following the KeyNote specification, IANA should provide a registry of reserved algorithm identifiers. This memo reserves six as public key and binary identifier encodings: rsa-hex, rsa-base64, dsa-hex, dsa-base64, binary-hex and binary-base64. It reserves six more as signature encodings: sig-rsa-md5-hex, sig-rsa-md5-base64, sig-rsa-sha1-hex, sig-rsa-sha1-base64, sig-dsa-sha1-hex and sig-dsa-sha1-base64. The double quotes used in the memo are not part of the algorithm identifiers.

The security section is short. The security of KeyNote credentials that use these keys depends directly on the strength of the underlying public key algorithms. On the security of KeyNote itself, the reader is referred to RFC 2704.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors asked for the label names to be written into an official list so that nobody uses the same label for something else. As for security, the memo says nothing beyond what the key algorithms already provide, and points at the KeyNote specification for the rest.
